title: Rust - like Thing Explainer

concepts.title: The Rust Promise
concepts.brief: Rust-specific concept: safety, performance, no GC. Explain the guarantees Rust aims for and the tradeoffs it asks developers to make. Establish the compiler as a correctness tool rather than an obstacle.

concepts.title: Ownership
concepts.brief: Rust-specific concept: move semantics, Drop, scopes. Who owns a value, why there can usually be one owner, what happens when ownership moves, and how deterministic cleanup works.

concepts.title: Borrowing
concepts.brief: Rust-specific concept: &T, &mut T, aliasing rules. Temporary access without ownership transfer. Explain the core rule: many readers or one writer, but not both.

concepts.title: Lifetimes Without Fear
concepts.brief: Rust-specific concept: reference validity, lifetime relationships. Show that lifetimes are Rust's way of proving references cannot outlive their data — not a manual memory-management mechanism.

concepts.title: Mutation and Interior Mutability
concepts.brief: Rust-specific concept: mut, Cell, RefCell, Mutex. Why Rust makes mutation explicit, when normal mutable references work, and why interior mutability introduces runtime checks or synchronization.

concepts.title: Modeling States With Enums
concepts.brief: Rust-specific concept: enum, Option, Result, pattern matching. Teach enums as the Rust-native way to represent alternatives, absence, state machines, and recoverable failure.

concepts.title: Pattern Matching as Proof
concepts.brief: Rust-specific concept: match, destructuring, exhaustiveness. Explain exhaustive matching as a correctness feature: Rust requires logic for every possible state.

concepts.title: Errors Are Values
concepts.brief: Rust-specific concept: Result, ?, custom errors. Distinguish expected errors from unrecoverable failures. Show propagation, contextual errors, and when panic! is appropriate.

concepts.title: Traits and Generic Constraints
concepts.brief: Rust-specific concept: traits, bounds, static/dynamic dispatch. Teach traits as capability contracts — not class inheritance — and show how generics express reusable behavior safely.

concepts.title: Shared Ownership and Smart Pointers
concepts.brief: Rust-specific concept: Box, Rc, Arc, Weak. Explain indirection, heap allocation, reference counting, cycles, and why shared ownership should be intentional.

concepts.title: Concurrency in the Type System
concepts.brief: Rust-specific concept: Send, Sync, threads, channels. Show how Rust prevents unsafe data sharing. Introduce ownership transfer between threads and safe shared state.

concepts.title: Async Is a Different Kind of Waiting
concepts.brief: Rust-specific concept: Future, async, .await, pinning intuition. Explain async as non-blocking suspension, not simply "threads with different syntax." Keep runtime details brief.

concepts.title: Unsafe and the Safe Boundary
concepts.brief: Rust-specific concept: unsafe, invariants, FFI. Explain why unsafe exists, what promises it requires, and how safe abstractions isolate its risk.

concepts.title: Thinking in Rust
concepts.brief: Rust-specific concept: design heuristics. A practical guide to interpreting borrow-checker feedback, reducing lifetime complexity, choosing ownership boundaries, and developing Rust intuition.

notes: Explain the Rust concepts that will be useful for a developer that is learning Rust. You can include SVG diagrams or animations if that will drive the point. Requested voice: Thing Explainer — explain complicated ideas using only the 1,000 most common English words. Word limit: only use very common, everyday words; if a technical term is unavoidable, introduce it once in quotes with a plain-word explanation (e.g., "this is called a 'lifetime'"), then go back to simple words. Concrete pictures over abstractions: every idea gets a real-world scene — friends, toys, paper, rooms, parties; the reader should be able to see it. One idea per chapter: explain a single concept fully, don't branch into related topics. Structure: start with the problem ("here is what goes wrong"), then the rule or fix, then why the fix is worth it. Acknowledge feelings: if something is famously annoying or confusing, say so — then show why it's still good. Tone: warm, patient, a little playful; short sentences; no jargon, no math notation, no code unless asked (code IS asked for here — this is a programming book, so show small code examples, but explain them in plain words). Chapter titles: rename the concept as a plain description — not "The Borrow Checker" but "The Strict Friend Who Checks All the Sharing Rules"; keep the plain-description title as the on-page chapter title while the table of contents may pair it with the concept name. End each chapter with one sentence about why this idea makes life better.
